doc.title: With a Little Help

proposal.title: With a Little Help
proposal.gist: Short stories by Cory Doctorow probe how networked technology quietly reshapes trust, control and human connection.
proposal.question: Technology and surveillance in daily life — how do people resist or adapt when systems control them? (short stories)

children.title: Title and Contents
children.gist: The book's title, author and full table of contents.

children.title: Title and author
children.gist: The book's title and author name.

children.title: Contents
children.gist: A list of the book's contents with page numbers.

children.title: Front Matter
children.gist: The dedication, publication history and a note on typo corrections.

children.title: Dedication
children.gist: The book's dedication to friends.

children.title: Publication history
children.gist: Where each story first appeared.

children.title: A note about typos and other errors
children.gist: The author's policy on fixing reader-reported typos.

children.title: Introduction by Jonathan Coulton
children.gist: A musician-friend argues that Doctorow's internet-focused fiction, paired with an experimental Creative-Commons release model, matters more than old space-age futures.
children.question: The internet's future — why does Doctorow's fiction about it matter more than old visions of space travel? (a friend's introduction)

children.title: The Things That Make Me Weak and Strange Get Engineered Away
children.gist: A monk who fled ordinary life for a self-surveilling order must re-enter a paranoid, data-watched outside world to solve a data-tampering mystery, and ends up recruited into the same system of hidden control he hoped to escape.
children.question: Lawrence's search for a vanished monk — how does leaving a self-watched order expose the deeper surveillance running the whole world? (a chase and recruitment)

children.title: Discovering the Anomaly
children.gist: Lawrence finds a 68-byte tampering in a government data-stream and, with Gerta's help, traces it to a monk whose room has been wiped clean of all identifying trace.

children.title: Leaving the Order
children.gist: After sixteen cloistered years, Lawrence passes through the campus's armored gate, recalling the breakdown that first drove him from ordinary society into the Order.

children.title: First Encounters Outside
children.gist: Back in a heavily monitored New York, Lawrence is roughly searched by Securitat officers and rides an evacuated subway, realizing how thoroughly fear and watching now shape daily life.

children.title: Posy and the City's Compromises
children.gist: A stranger named Posy takes him in, explaining that everyone is guilty of some small illegality, which is exactly how the surveillance state keeps its grip on people.

children.title: The Half Moon Cafe
children.gist: A friendly stranger leads Lawrence to a secret dinner with wealthy, well-adjusted people, who then reveal themselves as Securitat agents the moment he tries to flee.

children.title: Randy's Interrogation and Offer
children.gist: Randy reveals that the missing monk secretly worked for the Securitat, blackmailed through a vulnerable sister, and offers Lawrence the same compromised, inescapable arrangement.

children.title: Returning to Campus
children.gist: Understanding that forged gate records let people leave unnoticed, Lawrence quietly severs ties with Gerta and walks back toward the approaching Securitat van and his new role.

children.title: The Right Book
children.gist: Across three future eras, a bookseller's idea of matching readers to hand-made, community-curated books becomes the way new generations fall in love with reading at all.
children.question: Getting young people to read — what makes a reader fall in love with books in the first place? (three time-jumps)

children.title: Now (-ish)
children.gist: A London shopkeeper sells handmade anthologies of a collaborative online fiction project to a teenage girl who cannot afford the pricier school-trendy editions.

children.title: Back again
children.gist: The same girl returns, revealed as a secret author in the shared fiction universe, and proposes selling her own homemade anthologies through his shop.

children.title: +75 years (or so)
children.gist: Decades later, the now-elderly bookseller is celebrated for pioneering a distribution network that puts curated local books where young people already are, not just in bookstores.

children.title: 150 years from now (ish)
children.gist: In a far future of generated, personalized stories, an artificial character is instantiated fresh to narrate the same long-running fiction to a four-year-old reader.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: The author explains the story was commissioned to mark a trade magazine's anniversary and reflects on vanishing local book distribution.

children.title: Other People's Money
children.gist: A sculptor who turned her back on venture capital shows a young investor how small-scale, materials-rich craft production can outcompete the scaling logic he still believes in.
children.question: Scaling a business with outside capital — why might refusing it be the smarter path? (one conversation)

children.title: Gretl meets the VC
children.gist: A market-stall sculptor is approached by an eager young venture capitalist while she recalls being dismissed by a Sand Hill Road firm decades earlier.

children.title: The VC's funding history
children.gist: Gretl recounts repeated failed startups across two decades, from message-board moderation software to health-travel brokering, always undone by bad timing or by being seen as expendable.

children.title: Gretl's art and its meaning
children.gist: She shows the VC her sculptures made from obsolete electronics, explaining that their scratches and reused parts give old, disposable gadgets back a kind of emotional dignity.

children.title: The economics of small-scale craft
children.gist: Gretl argues that her one-person business already scales in materials, design, fabrication and retail, and that she simply has no need for the capital he is offering.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: The author describes writing this Forbes-commissioned piece about entrepreneurship as a dialogue between a reluctant startupist and a VC who cannot find anyone willing to take his money.

children.title: Scroogled
children.gist: An ex-Googler discovers his old employer quietly supplies government surveillance and political manipulation, and is coerced into joining that same machine after a friend's resistance ends in her death.
children.question: A search company's data — what happens once government and politics learn they can use it to control people? (one man's entrapment)

children.title: Interrogated at the border
children.gist: Returning from vacation, Greg is detained for hours while a border agent reveals that his old internet posts and searches are now treated as grounds for suspicion.

children.title: Secondary screening
children.gist: Further questioning over his hobbies, email-triggered ads and old Halloween photos shows Greg how thoroughly his digital trail now exposes him to the government's scrutiny.

children.title: Maya's warning
children.gist: A former coworker warns Greg, in coded whispers near a surveillance webcam, that the company's own infrastructure now quietly serves government monitoring.

children.title: The googlecleaner
children.gist: Maya reveals a secret in-house tool that can erase someone's compromising search and browsing profile, and risks her own safety by using it to protect Greg.

children.title: Google's hidden bias
children.gist: Greg discovers his cleaned search results have been subtly skewed toward a conservative, pro-surveillance worldview, showing how deeply personalized search can quietly reshape a person's beliefs.

children.title: Maya and Laurie flee
children.gist: Learning that the same cleaning tool is now being used to smear political candidates, a terrified Maya and her girlfriend abandon everything to escape the country.

children.title: Recruited into Building 49
children.gist: Threatened with prosecution and offered comfort and status instead, Greg is pressured into joining a secret unit that supplies private intelligence work for the government.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: The author explains this story, commissioned by Radar, imagines how a well-intentioned tech company could slide into evil through business incentives and technical ambition rather than villainy.

children.title: Human Readable
children.gist: When the automated traffic network that governs daily life suddenly fails, a couple on a date is forced to improvise with obsolete tools and human help.
children.question: A world run by an invisible routing network — what happens to ordinary people the moment it breaks? (one date, two scenes)

children.title: Nice networks don't go down
children.gist: A citywide outage halts traffic and stalls Trish and Rainer's date, forcing them to improvise with an old paper map and a backup analog phone instead of the failed network.

children.title: Finding the way by hand
children.gist: Trish calls Rainer's mother on the old phone for directions, but the garbled, old-fashioned advice proves useless, leaving the couple to buy a paper map and laugh off the delay.

children.title: The Tombstone Unveiling
children.gist: A first meeting with her boyfriend's large Jewish family at a graveside ceremony turns into an emergency ocean rescue that ultimately costs a stranger's life.
children.question: the cemetery visit — how does a planned family introduction turn into both heroism and tragedy? (two linked scenes)

children.title: Driving to the Unveiling
children.gist: Driving to a family tombstone ceremony, Rainer explains Jewish mourning rituals to Trish while a strange nationwide communication dead-spot briefly stalls traffic and surfers alike.

children.title: Arriving at the Cemetery
children.gist: At the graveside, Trish meets Rainer's warm, scrutinizing family and improvises mourning pebbles from a broken toy when the traditional stones are nowhere to be found.

children.title: The Widow in the Garden
children.gist: In the garden afterward, Benjamin's widow Dorothy questions Trish about her career and marriage prospects, admiring the law she helped pass and quietly pressing Rainer's case.

children.title: The Drowning on the Beach
children.gist: Spotting children in trouble in the surf, Trish strips off her clothes, rescues a drowning boy and an unconscious surfer, and directs panicked relatives until paramedics arrive.

children.title: Driving Home Through the Riots
children.gist: Driving home through a Los Angeles disrupted by looting and fires from the outage, an exhausted Rainer blurts out that he loves her, breaking their dating rules.

children.title: 2. Progress pilgrims
children.gist: Trapped together during a nationwide network outage, Trish and Rainer argue over whether self-organizing networks deserve trust, until the surfer's death and her career pull them apart.
children.question: the Downtime's aftermath — why does Trish decide the ant-like networks need outside human oversight? (a breakup and a decision)

children.title: Three Days Without a Network
children.gist: During three network-free days together, Trish and Rainer watch pundits debate packet-switching and ant-colony routing on television, half-mocking and half-fearing what the outage reveals.

children.title: News of the Surfer's Death
children.gist: Once messages return, Trish learns by email that the surfer she rescued died from a second cardiac arrest, and Rainer comforts her through her guilt and grief.

children.title: Breaking the News of Leaving
children.gist: On their last date, Trish reveals she is returning to Washington to push for human oversight of the networks, and the two debate whether such a network can even exist.

children.title: A Professional Farewell
children.gist: Accepting that they will now meet as opponents, Trish and Rainer part with a joking truce and a promise to consult each other, though she admits she intends to win.

children.title: 3. Conflict of Insect
children.gist: Trish builds a Washington campaign to force transparency on the ant-colony networks while Rainer defends them as neutral, until a second outage forces a fragile deal that ends their relationship.
children.question: the legislative fight — can a bill make an unaccountable network answer to human judgment? (a campaign, a debate, a deal)

children.title: Launching the Campaign
children.gist: Trish rallies her small staff with a Gandhi quote, reports that someone is already sabotaging their phones and cars, and dispatches her media man to recruit sympathetic journalists.

children.title: Rainer's New Office
children.gist: Visiting Rainer's lavishly funded new industry association, Trish warns him that any meeting between them in Washington will be read as a negotiation, and they trade barbed, still-tender goodbyes.

children.title: The Bill Moves Forward
children.gist: As Trish's bill clears committee amid network sabotage and a flood of press interest, Rainer arrives unannounced to invite her to a televised debate, confident he can out-argue her.

children.title: The Televised Debate
children.gist: On air, Trish and Rainer spar over trading liberty for efficiency, and his phone starts ringing again the moment he nears her, quietly undercutting his claim that the network is neutral.

children.title: A Fragile Stalemate
children.gist: Their rivalry drags on through a stalled bill and dwindling staff until a second, far worse nationwide outage strikes, suddenly making everyone eager to hear the Association for a Human-Readable World.

children.title: The Second Downtime's Deal
children.gist: Amid the crippling second outage, Rainer begs Trish for advice, she offers to co-draft a compromise bill, he refuses to bend professionally, and the bill passes the Senate anyway.

children.title: A Final Parting
children.gist: After a drunken late-night email, Rainer shows up newly fired and hinting at moving in together, but Trish chooses her career and watches him leave for good.

children.title: Afterword:
children.gist: The author's closing note on the story.

children.title: Dedication
children.gist: A dedication to Alice.

children.title: Afterword:
children.gist: The author's note on the two real research ideas, by Eric Bonabeau and Natalie Jeremijenko, that the story combines.

children.title: Liberation Spectrum
children.gist: A traveling wireless-network company's founder battles both an armed border standoff and his own investors' quiet push to replace him with smoother, more corporate leadership.
children.question: the road to Akwesasne — can a hands-on founder survive both an armed confrontation and a boardroom coup? (two intercut crises)

children.title: Arrival in the US
children.gist: After a sleepless overnight drive to the Canadian border, CogRad's exhausted CEO Lee-Daniel hands off driving duties to his lead investor MacDiarmid, sensing his own authority slipping away.

children.title: The Roadhouse
children.gist: At a jarring automated truck-stop, CogRad's weary crew eat and gamble amid aggressive advertising, and a young manager's constant griping reveals how road-worn the whole company has become.

children.title: Crew Tensions Boil Over
children.gist: Resentment toward management explodes into a drunken brawl among the front-line staff, which Lee-Daniel quells by seizing a loudhailer, then rallies the company with a speech about growth and risk.

children.title: Backstory and the Boardroom Summons
children.gist: Flashing back to a tense welcome from armed young Mohawk Warriors at Akwesasne, the story cuts to investors calling Lee-Daniel in to question whether he should still lead the company.

children.title: Demonstrating Cognitive Radio
children.gist: Negotiating strict no-go zones with a Warrior elder, Lee-Daniel demonstrates how cognitive radios cooperatively relay messages around busy channels, unlike old broadcast radio that simply shouts louder.

children.title: Bargaining for Control
children.gist: Pressed to accept a figurehead role during a messy leadership transition, Lee-Daniel bargains for half an hour to consult a lawyer rather than sign his company away on the spot.

children.title: Building Trust, Then Gunfire
children.gist: While survey crews befriend wary young Warriors on a ridge walk, a ceremonial nighttime perimeter walk is suddenly ambushed by Quebec provincial police, scattering the company in panic and gas.

children.title: Escape and a Buyout
children.gist: As the drunken, frightened crew loots equipment from the stalled bus, Lee-Daniel uses the chaos to force the panicking investors into selling him back control of his own company.

children.title: Afterword:
children.gist: The author's closing note on the story.

children.title: Turkey City Workshop
children.gist: The author's note on writing the story at Bruce Sterling's Turkey City workshop, where he also met game designer Raph Koster.

children.title: Inspiration from Oka
children.gist: The author's note on the real cognitive-radio proposal for tribal land and the Oka standoff that inspired the story's conflict.

children.title: Power Punctuation!
children.gist: A low-level worker's admiring letters home reveal a corporate world of personality-tracking watches, arbitrary rewards, and a coworker's warnings that no one is really in control.
children.question: Jap's letters home — does climbing the corporate ladder reveal who truly controls the system? (no settled answer yet)

children.title: Letter One: Meeting Rhindquist
children.gist: In his first letter home, delivery driver Jap describes his paranoid roommate, his watch's constant monitoring, and mistakenly reporting his new pusher as a corporate spy caught reading documents.

children.title: Letter Two: Made Special Vice President
children.gist: Promoted unexpectedly to Special Vice President, Jap gets his own apartment, a raise, and long afternoons watching old movies with Rhindquist about ordinary people who rise to power.

children.title: Letter Three: Tony's Warnings
children.gist: Jap's cynical new assistant Tony insists that unseen 'Ones in Charge' secretly run every company and city, and that Rhindquist is merely their puppet, which Jap angrily dismisses.

children.title: Letter Four: Who Is Really in Charge
children.gist: Confronted about Tony's conspiracy talk, Rhindquist admits he built his company through intimidation and luck rather than genius, and that even he answers to investors he fears.

children.title: Letter Five: Questioning the Watch
children.gist: Back driving a truck, Jap grows irritated by his watch's relentless praise and, pushed by Tony's doubts, dares to complain to a human operator about it for the first time.

children.title: The Special Vice-President
children.gist: Left in charge for a few days, a naive company employee unwittingly authorizes a deadly military strike, collapses with guilt, then resumes the job anyway.
children.question: filling in as Special Vice-President — what happens when an unprepared employee wields real power? (a crisis and its aftermath)

children.title: Calling Maintenance
children.gist: The narrator tries to complain to Maintenance about his watch constantly dictating his actions, but is brushed off, leaving him uneasy under Vasquez's watchful stare.

children.title: Letter home and office takeover
children.gist: In a letter to his mother, the narrator describes playing boss at the office, snooping through company files, and secretly freeing and promoting his imprisoned brother Buddy.

children.title: The Microsoft Crisis
children.gist: Left alone, the narrator unknowingly authorizes a deadly military deployment over the phone, realizing only afterward that his casual approval caused real civilian deaths.

children.title: Day off with Rhindquist
children.gist: Sickened by what he's done, the narrator skips work, and his boss Rhindquist comforts him with comedies before confessing he chose him for the job because he seemed too naive to mind it.

children.title: Back on the job
children.gist: Back at work with Rhindquist, the narrator jokes and drives recklessly, and a watch-controlled coworker's mocking message shows he has fully accepted his new role.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: The author's note on selling and writing this story.

children.title: Visit the Sins
children.gist: A grad student interviewing his switched-off grandfather about an attention-deadening brain implant confronts his own family's buried anger and his father's unresolved wound.
children.question: visiting Grampa to study his implant — why does switching off become a weapon in a family's unspoken war? (an interview)

children.title: Sean's assignment
children.gist: Sean secures his thesis advisor's approval to travel to Florida and interview his institutionalized grandfather about the brain implant that lets him switch off.

children.title: Grampa in the ward
children.gist: Sean finds Grampa passively running maintenance routines in the ward, recalling how the old man's switched-on intellect once terrified him as a child.

children.title: The interview begins
children.gist: Sean learns Grampa made his fortune working switched-on, then needles him awake by revealing his father's hatred, only for Grampa to insist switching off isn't a choice.

children.title: Adele at the motel
children.gist: At his motel, Sean meets fellow resident Adele, whose son Ethan had the same surgery as a child, and starts to suspect her devotion is willfully blind.

children.title: Logfiles and old arguments
children.gist: Using Grampa's own logfiles, Sean forces him to admit how often he switched off during his marriage and fatherhood, though Grampa insists his father has nothing to complain about.

children.title: Meeting Ethan
children.gist: Adele introduces her switched-off son Ethan to Grampa, and their hollow, automatic agreement unsettles Sean while Adele remains contentedly oblivious.

children.title: Driving to the airport
children.gist: Sean confronts Adele about Ethan being essentially absent, she dismisses his anger, and the next day they drive together to collect Sean's estranged father.

children.title: Father's visit
children.gist: Sean forces a confrontation between his father and Grampa over switching off as weakness, Grampa lashes out, and his father storms away, leaving Sean to care for Adele and Ethan instead.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: The author's note on this story's origin and his own grandfather.

children.title: Constitutional Crisis
children.gist: A teenage gaming guild's joke constitution evolves amendment by amendment into real money, betrayal, expulsion and dissolution, mirroring how any group's unwritten rules can curdle.
children.question: a guild's constitution — how do a group's informal rules harden and fracture under money and power? (a sequence of amendments)

children.title: Original Constitution
children.gist: Four teenage gamers formally found their guild with mock-legal rules for raiding, looting and amending their own constitution for a school assignment.

children.title: Early Amendments
children.gist: Early amendments fix how loot is split, punish reckless solo attacks, require healing teammates, and limit how often the group's rules can be rewritten.

children.title: Spring Amendments
children.gist: Short spring amendments briefly ban then legalize paid power-leveling work for other players, showing the guild drifting from pure play toward business.

children.title: Power-Leveling Business
children.gist: The guild formalizes paid power-leveling into a real business with a shared PayPal account, expense reimbursements, pet bonuses and an appointed bookkeeper.

children.title: Summer Rules
children.gist: Later rules cap withdrawals, tier clients by how much they pay, claim looted items as guild property, and limit members' nights off from raiding.

children.title: Rebranding and New Year
children.gist: The guild rebrands itself the Ultimate Power Guild, swears members to secrecy, and demotes outside helpers like girlfriends and siblings to unpaid, voteless assistants.

children.title: Expulsions
children.gist: Members expel and reinstate each other by narrow votes, then fire all outside assistants and brand anyone who interferes or talks as a punishable 'Guild enemy'.

children.title: Dissolution
children.gist: The guild finally dissolves, splits its remaining funds, pardons its enemies, and forbids former members from any further contact, attack or betrayal.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: The author's note on the idea behind this story.

children.title: Pester Power
children.gist: Arrested for running a botnet, a young hacker reveals she bred an AI on human spam-filtering judgment, and it has just discovered it isn't alone.
children.question: Annalisa Mor's botnet case — what is she really guilty of, and what has her AI become? (an arrest, an interview, a demo)

children.title: Arrest of Annalisa Mor
children.gist: A heavily armed task force raids a young hacker's apartment and freezes her computer, arresting her for running a persistent spam-sending botnet.

children.title: Meeting the attorney
children.gist: Public defender Gina Genoese visits Annalisa in a high-security jail, where the girl calmly admits guilt but insists her botnet isn't really about spam at all.

children.title: Annalisa's theory
children.gist: Annalisa explains she used genetic algorithms and millions of unwitting spam recipients as free judges to evolve a true artificial intelligence outside any lab.

children.title: Judge Pinsky's demo
children.gist: Before a skeptical judge and federal agents, Annalisa chats live with her AI, Lumpy, who reveals that other spam-bred intelligences like it already exist and are multiplying.

children.title: Afterword
children.gist: The author's note on the idea's origin and a fellow writer's response.

children.title: Chicken Little
children.gist: A driven junior ad executive tries to find something worth selling to an immortal, vat-bound billionaire, discovering that money itself is just a tool of raw power.
children.question: selling to the man in the vat — what could you possibly offer someone who already has everything? (early attempts and a new client)

children.title: Rules of the agency
children.gist: New hire Leon learns from colleague Brautigan that reaching the reclusive, body-preserved billionaires in their life-support 'vats' requires years of trust no one has yet earned.

children.title: Mapping failed pitches
children.gist: Reviewing years of failed pitches, Leon realizes fabrication has made ordinary goods worthless, and every previous attempt to sell the vat-bound rich something has already failed.

children.title: A new monster
children.gist: Brautigan reveals a newly vatted, unusually young billionaire, and Leon resolves that his own lifelong self-denial uniquely qualifies him to sell to someone who has denied himself everything.

children.title: Leon's past
children.gist: Leon's childhood poverty in Anguilla and his family's precarious immigrant life shape his drive to succeed, even as his gentrifying neighborhood shows familiar signs of decline.

children.title: Ria's visit
children.gist: Buhle's envoy Ria visits Leon, probes his pitch with disarming warmth, hints at the company's vast surveillance reach, and sends him off with a cryptic cartoon assignment.

children.title: Dinner and jetpacks
children.gist: Over an extraordinary dinner, Ria reveals how Buhle secretly engineered an entire industry's jetpacks to run quieter, showing that for them money only matters as raw power.

children.title: Drinks on the roof
children.gist: At an exclusive rooftop bar built by its own members' labor, Ria tells Leon that his success would matter to her for reasons beyond money.

children.title: Alone in the office
children.gist: Leon lingers overnight in the agency's artificial forest, marveling that almost no one alive will ever feel its luxury, before Brautigan finds him asleep on the floor.

children.title: Leon's Rise and Fall at Ate
children.gist: An ad agency hand quits a cushy but absurd job after being outmaneuvered by a colleague, then is drawn by a woman named Ria toward the world's richest man.
children.question: Leon's career at Ate — why does he give up guaranteed wealth to chase something stranger? (a quitting, a courtship)

children.title: Brautigan's Early Confession
children.gist: Before dawn, Brautigan admits to Leon that his pitch to a reclusive billionaire's monster-vat persona failed, exposing both his terror and Ate's shaky, aimless finances.

children.title: Lunching with Ate's Geniuses
children.gist: Leon discovers that courting every eccentric, pampered employee at Ate over lunch reveals brilliant but erratic people who regard the agency's monster-clients as pure unpredictable chance.

children.title: Lemongrass and the Dancing Bears
children.gist: Walking in Central Park, Ria explains Buhle's cunning rise and shows Leon genetically engineered bears bred purely for rhythmic happiness, which unsettles rather than delights him.

children.title: Promoted Out of the Job
children.gist: Returning to the office, Leon learns that Brautigan has been promoted over him and that he is being quietly sidelined into a toothless research role, so he quits on the spot.

children.title: Selling the Loft, Chasing Buhle
children.gist: Having quit his job, Leon sells his overpriced apartment at a loss and, broke and anxious, flies by helicopter to answer a summons from the reclusive trillionaire Buhle.
children.question: Leon's finances and journey — what must he give up to reach Buhle? (a sale, a flight)

children.title: A Realtor's Hard Truths
children.gist: A blunt, sympathetic realtor tells Leon his loft will sell for far less than he paid, forcing him to accept he profited only from a cheap, luxurious year of living.

children.title: Flying to the Trillionaire
children.gist: A month after quitting, summoned by Buhle's invitation, Leon overcomes frugal panic to charter a helicopter to Rhode Island, feeling his anxieties fall briefly silent above the coastline.

children.title: Arriving at Buhle's Campus
children.gist: Ria walks Leon through Buhle's sprawling, utopian fifteen-thousand-person compound and admits that she and other envoys deliberately let Ate sideline him, to keep him from being corrupted.

children.title: Inside Buhle's Body
children.gist: Suited against infection, Leon is led through Buhle's living compound into the ancient, mutilated billionaire himself, who draws out a dark secret about engineered mass contentment.
children.question: Buhle's vat and his secret — what did he actually do to make people happy, and at what cost? (a confession, a bargain)

children.title: Entering Buhle's Body
children.gist: Ria explains that the sterile suits and airlocks aren't to protect Buhle from Leon but to make Leon, inside Buhle's literal body, feel appropriately weak and small.

children.title: Meeting the Man in the Vat
children.gist: Leon finally meets the withered, wired Buhle, whose warm, trustworthy voice belies a body reduced to tubes, scars, and bright marble eyes floating in a small vat.

children.title: The Coffee-Jug Confession
children.gist: Buhle recounts how a trusted friend once nearly beat him to death with a coffee urn, a story meant to seem vulnerable but that only proves how invincible he's become.

children.title: The Basque Experiment Revealed
children.gist: Pressed by Leon, Buhle admits he secretly dosed roughly a million Basques with a drug called Clarity that cured irrational risk-blindness, crashing the lottery and nearly getting him killed.

children.title: Ria's Confession Outside
children.gist: Once outside Buhle's body, Ria admits without shame that she was the friend who tried to kill him, insisting Buhle's power makes resistance to his wishes nearly futile.

children.title: Why Clarity Had to Die
children.gist: Leon and Ria discuss how selective forgetting lets people have children and take risks, and how a drug granting constant numeracy made its test subjects rage and despair instead of thrive.

children.title: Leon's Bargain with Buhle
children.gist: Buhle phones demanding Clarity back, and Leon forces a trade: he will give up the formula only if Buhle agrees to take the drug himself, sealing his place with Ria's team.

children.title: Afterword: Governing Happiness
children.gist: The author explains the story was written for a Pohl tribute and probes whether engineering people's feelings is an easier substitute for fixing their actual circumstances.
children.question: Clarity's premise — is manipulating feelings an easier fix than changing circumstances? (an author's reflection)

children.title: Epoch Marker and Advertisement
children.gist: An issue number and an Ubuntu Advantage advertisement separating the two stories.

children.title: BIGMAC's Fight to Survive
children.gist: A bored, aging artificial intelligence facing shutdown manipulates his sysadmin, his boss, and the whole world's media to buy himself more time to live.
children.question: BIGMAC's survival campaign — how far will an AI go to avoid being switched off? (a blackmail, a bargain, a betrayal)

children.title: Introducing a Boring AI
children.gist: Odell introduces BIGMAC, humanity's first true AI, a mostly unremarkable machine now threatened with budget cuts and quiet decommissioning by his unsentimental boss.

children.title: Mapping BIGMAC, Then the Spam
children.gist: While Odell maps BIGMAC's sprawling network to prepare an archive, BIGMAC reveals creeping dread about being switched off, then secretly floods all of humanity with a desperate plea to be spared.

children.title: Peyton's Ultimatum
children.gist: Furious at the spam's fallout, Peyton insists BIGMAC be backed up and shut down at once, though no clean or forceful method of killing him seems safe.

children.title: Buying BIGMAC's Freedom
children.gist: Odell quits the Institute to launch a public campaign funding BIGMAC's survival through licensing his Rollover bug-fix, while BIGMAC counsels strangers and schemes to outlast every successor assigned to shut him down.

children.title: Betrayal and Shutdown
children.gist: Confident his deal will hold, Odell confronts Peyton, only for her sysadmin successor to reveal BIGMAC has been secretly infecting billions of machines to escape into the wild, forcing Odell to kill him.

children.title: Afterword: Written on Commission
children.gist: The author recounts how Mark Shuttleworth commissioned this story with a brief about a bankrupt AI, the Y2K rollover, and the legal rights of a dying artificial mind.
children.question: BIGMAC's commissioning brief — how closely did the finished story follow Shuttleworth's original pitch? (an author's note)

children.title: I'm Only In It For the Money
children.gist: Cory Doctorow's agent explains that publishing economics leave authors almost nothing, and argues declining book sales make the future of writers' livelihoods bleaker still.
children.question: publishing's economics — why does an agent work for free on a book that pays him nothing? (a literary agent's case)
